0f9890a728a058e8.content_excerpt: What a 35-point benchmark cliff, a slowdown study nobody wanted to publish, and real 2026 payroll data say about replacing engineers with agents Claude Opus 4.8 clears 88.6% on SWE-bench Verified . That's the number everyone quotes to argue AI has basically solved software engineering. Now drop it into SWE-bench Pro — the version built from private codebases the model has never seen. The best standardized score on the public leaderboard is 59.1%. On the truly private commercial set, where nobody gets to tune in advance, no model clears 47%. That's not a rounding error. That's a 20-to-40-point cliff, and it shows up everywhere. Gemini 3.1 Pro falls from 80.6% to somewhere between 32% and 46%, depending on which cut you trust. Every lab's flagship shows the same shape of fall. Here's a wrinkle nobody saw coming: the two highest-scoring models that exist right now — Claude Mythos 5 (95.5%) and Claude Fable 5 (95.0%) — aren't something you can actually use. Anthropic suspended public access to both under an export control directive. The "best" model on paper this week is one you can't buy. That gap, between the benchmark you can quote and the codebase you actually own, is the entire "AI replaces developers" argument in miniature. Models are extraordinary at problems that resemble what they've already seen. We measured that cost for six CLIs: start-up, time per turn, memory, image size and tokens. On overhead per job, pi was the lightest overall. Our own CLI, aictrl , won no metric but came second on four: session time, harness time per turn, memory and image size. Overhead is half the answer: this experiment does not measure whether an agent completes the task, which our next run will. Goose had the fastest observed median first response, followed by Codex, pi and aictrl. Those four were within 187 ms of each other. pi used the fewest tokens, both in its first request and for a whole short task, spent the least time between model turns, added the least image footprint and finished the scripted session fastest. aictrl came second on session time, per-turn harness time, memory and image footprint. Its system prompt is now as small as pi's. Its tool definitions are not. Each chart is sorted from lowest to highest, with gold and silver medals for the observed first and second place on that metric. A medal describes this experiment; small gaps do not establish a stable lead. Disclosure: I build aictrl. This article reports our own measurements, including where our implementation loses. 30905c664e5a48e8.content_excerpt: ARD is an open discovery protocol for agentic resources ( GitHub ). It allows an AI client to ask: "What is available for this task?" and lets a discovery service answer with matching resources. ARD sits entirely before invocation. It helps the client find the right resource; the resource is then invoked through its own native mechanism. An agentic resource is any external capability an AI client can call on to do a task — an agent, MCP server, Skill, Canvas, Plugin, API, or workflow — anything that can be described as an ARD entry . It is not an execution runtime: ARD is not MCP, A2A, Skills, AI Catalog, or an API runtime, and it does not replace them. It is not a central catalog: There will be many discovery services, each indexing different resources, serving different communities, and applying its own trust, ranking, and access policies. Every enterprise can run its own — much like an intranet has its own search engine over internal content. And on the public web there will be many, some optimizing for quality and trust, others for coverage. ARD is being developed by a working group with participants from Microsoft, Google, Hugging Face, GoDaddy, and others. This work is part of a broader effort to create an open discovery layer for resources that AIs can draw on. Agentic Resource Discovery (ARD) and its resources are licensed under the Apache License 2.0 and welcomes contributions from the community.

48e620c754016698.content_excerpt: Passwordless authentication via DID signatures. No passwords. No sessions. Nothing to breach. The cryptographic core of ArkenForge. ECDSA signature verification, did:key identity, nonce generation. arken-core is the Rust library that everything in ArkenForge builds on. It handles: It compiles to a native shared library ( .dylib / .so / .dll ) loaded by higher-level packages via FFI. All functions write JSON into out and return the number of bytes written, or -1 on buffer overflow. An unsigned request gets a 401 with a one-time nonce. The client signs the nonce with its secp256k1 private key and retries with an Authorization: Signature header. The core verifies the ECDSA signature, checks the nonce, and returns the agent's did:key — nothing stored, nothing breached. The zQ3s… prefix indicates secp256k1 ( 0xe7 0x01 multicodec). Same key, same DID, across every server running Arken. One identity, every tool. See SECURITY.md . Find a flaw, open a private advisory, and your name goes in the Hall of Finders. Founding Builders — everyone who joins before December 15, 2026 — are credited by name in the 1.0 README. There are 10 design-partner slots for teams who want to shape the API directly. Passwordless authentication via DID signatures. No passwords. No sessions. Nothing to breach.

4eb8a6cb7861fe9d.content_excerpt: QwenPU is Qwen3.5-4B with a 32-bit RISC-V CPU and a vector unit compiled into its weights. The vector unit runs a whole neural network inside the model's forward passes: Andrej Karpathy's stories260K , the 260K-parameter Llama from llama2.c , runs as a program on it and writes its stories. It's part of Qwenputer : the same CPU, compiled into transformer layers in front of Qwen's own, every weight set by a compiler, with Qwen3.5's Gated DeltaNet state as its memory. Qwenputer-npu gave that CPU dot-product instructions. QwenPU gives it a vector unit of its own: separate memories in DeltaNet heads, 64-lane matrix rows a token, and whole vector results streamed through the token stream. Work in progress. QwenPU is exact, but not yet small: the checkpoint is 26.7 GB, so it needs a 40 GB or larger GPU to load whole. The story demo and the checks run the computer's layers on their own and fit a 24 GB GPU. Trimming the hidden size, and with it the checkpoint, is next. stories260K is a C program here ( guests/stories260k/stories_vx.c ). Its int4 weights sit in the vector unit's weight memory, loaded from the program, and every matrix row, residual add, softmax and attention read is a vector op. None of it is compiled into the checkpoint, so any model that fits runs the same way. Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the park. 544129c2e0dc4a89.content_excerpt: I asked an AI coding agent to fix a bug in the RISC-V An open instruction set architecture. Many open-source processor cores implement it. processor inside Caliptra A large open-source system on chip from CHIPS Alliance. It is a hardware root of trust: a security block with its own RISC-V processor and firmware. . It usually found the faulty line of RTL Register-transfer level: the code that describes a chip’s hardware, usually written in Verilog or SystemVerilog. A simulator runs it; synthesis tools turn it into gates. within five minutes. Proving the fix took much longer, because the agent first had to make the bug show up in simulation. Over ten trials, two hardware-specific problems took most of that time: the internal signals that explain a failure are invisible unless the simulation records them, and simulations run long enough that the agent has to guess when they finish. A third problem, a build that depends on settings the agent's shell doesn't keep, isn't specific to hardware but is common in RTL projects. With tools aimed at all three, the same agent's mean time to a verified fix fell from 56 minutes to 21. Coding agents are built mostly for software work. Their working loop assumes that a test runs in seconds, that a failure prints a useful message, and that a command is cheap to rerun. Hardware design breaks all three. It came to 31 files and about 1,700 changed lines, with a two-sentence description. GitHub listed the files alphabetically, so the review opened on a CI config change, and the migration every other file depended on sat below five API files. PRs this size are becoming routine. At Rails World in September, David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH) said 37signals now has agents writing nearly all of its code. Generating code is now cheap, and the human attention needed to review it is what runs out. Thanks for reading ByteSizedBets! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. Keeping PRs small is still the best fix. Agents don’t reliably do it, though, and some changes are large by nature, like a schema migration or a rename across the whole repo. This issue is about reviewing those well. We also planted nine problems in the PR, from a privilege escalation to a behavior change hidden inside a moved file, so we could see what the tooling caught and what it missed. The walkthrough below uses CodeRabbit Explain , and every screenshot comes from that PR. Where plain git covers part of the job, I’ve included the commands. 6d8a8ee7d8dd93df.content_excerpt: For the past two years, building capable Agents meant designing tools, figuring out which actions help the model complete a task, deciding how granular each tool schema needs to be, or iterating on system instruction templates. This is changing. Agents are moving in the opposite direction by collapsing their entire tool catalog into one tool : exec . This is called Code Mode (or Programmatic Tool Calling). Instead of forcing the model to trigger tools one at a time across turns, the harness gives the model a single exec(code) tool. The model writes a short TypeScript or Python script that chains, combines, and awaits actions inside an isolated sandbox. To understand why agents are converging on a single exec tool, we should look at how tool calling evolved. Initially, we only gave agents a handful of tools because they couldn't reliably choose or filter across a large catalog. As models improved, we connected dozens of tools or MCP servers, but ran into context window limits. We solved that with tool search and progressive disclosure , letting agents look up tools on demand. Even with dynamic tool loading, we still had dozens of individual tools, and were still stuck with the limitation of standard tool calling: one action per turn. Generative AI tools excel at increasing coding speed, but pure speed without structured guardrails means we are often auto-scaling our mistakes rather than simply writing code faster. We need a paradigm shift, aligning the human need for system comprehension with AI’s capacity for execution. As co-author Dave Rensin outlines in the article Elephants, Goldfish, and the New Golden Age of Software Engineering , “Design is the new code.” The EGM framework is a metaphor for a powerful way to develop AI-assisted software quickly and safely with humans intentionally in the loop. The “Elephant” is a context-rich, long-horizon AI session that holds the end-to-end architectural vision and project memory. No code is written here; it is purely dedicated to design, intent, and capturing micro-decisions. The Elephant session is where the AI interviews you and you debate the merits of your choices. 967be99077d13f07.content_excerpt: One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users ( DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade” , Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture , and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway). For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX . In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. ( Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.) But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. Whenever I read one of these accounts, I think to myself, “Where are the benchmarks?” Well I got curious, so I wr

a7b3995f39a11035.content_excerpt: rufous is an agent harness for 2B–12B models running on your own machine, either inside your editor or in its own web UI. While the model works, rufous keeps a Record of every Tool Call, one the model has no way of editing. Before a Turn ends, we hold the model’s report up against that Record. That is how we catch the file you named that never got written, the write you declined, and the refusal the model only half remembers. There is a single binary for macOS and Linux, and a zip for Windows. rufous is licensed under Apache-2.0, and you won’t need an account. Nothing about your usage is sent back to us. The short of it, is that rufous is built around the limits of a small model. We have measured it on models between 2B and 12B parameters, and every run starts with a Prefill of about 1,250 tokens , i.e. the system prompt plus nine core tool schemas. Every Tool Call the model makes passes through the five Rings of the Safety Gate before it touches your system. When a Turn ends with something missing, rufous places one Hold on the reply at most, and an honest “I couldn’t” always passes. Give a 4B model one clear instruction and it will usually carry it out. Three Turns into a conversation however, it turns out that it often does something close to what you asked, and then reports success. This is because a small model follows the most recent text in front of it, not the state of your files. rufous can’t make the model remember. What it can do is check. Every Tool Call is writte

b78023b26122d472.content_excerpt: Claude Haiku scored 82% on 21 MCP servers through OpenCode and 65% through Claude Code. The gap comes from the built-in tools each agent reaches for first. We ran the same model, Claude Haiku 5.5, through two coding agents against the same 21 MCP servers, with the agent as the only difference. Through OpenCode it answered 82.0% of the tasks correctly from the server. Through Claude Code it answered 65.4%. We were testing M3 , our open-source tool for testing MCP servers , and wanted a workload big enough to break it: 21 real servers, about 20 tasks each, three agents, three trials per task. The results became the MCP Agent Usability leaderboard , and every number in this post comes from it. Our first guess was that OpenCode is simply better at calling tools. Splitting the servers by what they do rules that out. Eleven of the servers do a job none of the agents has a built-in tool for: a Postgres database, MongoDB, Redis, Kafka, Linear, Jenkins, Grafana, Kubernetes, Gitea, and two browser servers. The other ten overlap with something every agent already carries: web search and docs lookup (Exa, Fetch, Microsoft Learn, DeepWiki, Terraform), files and shell (Git, Filesystem, Desktop Commander, Serena), and memory. On the first eleven, the three agents land within 4.1 points of each other, even though Codex runs a different model. On the other ten, Claude Code trails OpenCode by 32 points and Codex trails it by 49. Here is one task from the Exa server, run once through each agent

b836eb939c37ffa5.content_excerpt: Generating tokens faster starts with identifying what limits inference performance. In the batch-size-1 evaluation of Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI on NVIDIA DGX Spark, profiling showed that decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out—the mixture-of-experts (MoE) computation and the output-layer projection that produces scores across the model’s vocabulary. Those findings pointed to two ways to improve performance: reduce the weight traffic in each decode step and generate more tokens per verification round. This post examines three techniques that address those costs: This post explains how each optimization works, measures its effect, and examines an integration issue that can make the combined configuration slower than the baseline. Ling-3.0-flash serves as the implementation example, with code and deployment instructions in the Ling cookbook . The evaluation used Ling-3.0-flash-fp4, a mixture-of-experts model with 124 billion total parameters and 5.1 billion active parameters per token. The model has 42 layers: 35 Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) linear-attention layers and seven multi-head latent attention (MLA) layers. Each MoE layer routes each token to eight of 512 routed experts, alongside one shared expert. For agentic workflows, Ling-3.0-flash provides a native 256K-token context window, expandable to 1M tokens. Compared with the previous Ling flash model, it improves long-horizon task stability, tool-calling accurac

baaa37d6dddd5d25.content_excerpt: Deterministic code dictionary for LLMs and developers: tree-sitter + SQLite, no AI. Cuts Claude Code token use by answering code questions from an index. A dictionary of your code for the AI, and a manual for you. It reads your project once, with no AI, and hands the answer over together with the question. Fewer turns, fewer tokens, the same correct answer. One line, once per machine. It also turns codedict on in Claude Code for every project. That's it. Open Claude Code in any git repository and ask about the code. There is nothing else to configure. Uninstall: run ~/.codedict/venv/bin/python -m codedict setup --remove (Windows: ~\.codedict\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m codedict setup --remove ) and delete the ~/.codedict folder. codedict came from a practical problem: on a real project with ~250 files in TypeScript, C# and Python, Claude Code sessions kept hitting the usage limit. We measured it, and the culprit was not the code being read but the number of turns . Every time the AI calls a tool (a grep, opening a file), Claude Code re-reads the whole context: 35 to 50 thousand tokens per turn. A simple question like "where is X and who calls it?" took 5 turns of grep and file reads. A flow question like "from the click to the result" took more than 20. The idea was to do the search work once, with no AI , in a local index, and hand the ready answer over together with the question. The AI answers in 1 or 2 turns instead of 5 to 20. cfe6b1639c3c3094.content_excerpt: Context window optimization for AI coding agents. Sandboxes tool output (98% reduction), persists session memory, and enforces routing across 17 platforms via MCP + hooks. Every MCP tool call dumps raw data into your context window. A Playwright snapshot costs 56 KB. Twenty GitHub issues cost 59 KB. One access log — 45 KB. After 30 minutes, 40% of your context is gone. And when the agent compacts the conversation to free space, it forgets which files it was editing, what tasks are in progress, and what you last asked for. On top of that, the agent wastes output tokens on filler, pleasantries, and verbose explanations — burning context from both sides. Context Saving — Sandbox tools keep raw data out of the context window. 315 KB becomes 5.4 KB. 98% reduction. Session Continuity — Every file edit, git operation, task, error, and user decision is tracked in SQLite. When the conversation compacts, context-mode doesn't dump this data back into context — it indexes events into FTS5 and retrieves only what's relevant via BM25 search. The model picks up exactly where you left off. If you don't --continue , previous session data is deleted immediately — a fresh session means a clean slate. Think in Code — The LLM should program the analysis, not compute it. Instead of reading 50 files into context to count functions, the agent writes a script that does the counting and console.log() s only the result. One script replaces ten tool calls and saves 100x context. This is a mandatory para

d8b1c52ddd336825.content_excerpt: GDPx is a benchmark that covers the most valuable domains for frontier intelligence. It aims to be the world’s best benchmark for measuring general agentic capabilities. We believe the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI , not broadly diffused throughout the whole economy. Building a general-purpose benchmark based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy is therefore a mistake. If your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment—the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in—you get the following results instead. We were pleasantly surprised by how well this ranking lines up with our subjective impression of the models. OpenAI and Anthropic generally dominate the top of the ranking while SpaceXAI, Meta, and open-weight models are all meaningfully behind. Gemini 4 Carbon is a real improvement from Google and the only model in the same ballpark as Opus and Astra. It will be interesting to see people’s impressions once Carbon becomes generally available. dbaecb6c683e8493.content_excerpt: Adversarial agent loops (producer, worker, gatekeeper) so agents do routine work and humans make the key decisions devloops gives a coding agent three loops: producer , worker , and gatekeeper . Each loop is a skill ( SKILL.md plus helper scripts). You install the skills into a project's .agents/skills/ directory. A per-project file, devloops.config.yaml , holds the project values (repo, branches, commands, protected paths, labels). Most maintenance work is routine: find a problem, write an issue, fix it, review the fix. devloops lets agents do that routine work in an adversarial loop : The worker and the gatekeeper go back and forth until the gatekeeper approves. The human does not do this routine work. The human makes only the important decisions: A scheduler starts each loop in ticks . Before a worker tick starts the agent, tick_gate.py decides if there is anything to do: So a change that happens during a tick is never hidden, and only an idle, unchanged state gives NOOP . The producer has its own gate, producer_gate.py . It picks the most overdue task ( --next ) from the task periods in the config. It does not overwrite a skill that already exists. Add the state directory (default .devloops/ ) to .gitignore . Check the prerequisites first (Python, GitHub API, git , gh auth , push permission): /gatekeeper-loop and /producer-loop use the same forms. /gatekeeper-loop 10m --pr N reviews one PR. /producer-loop runs one producer task. e6077e10f16ce2d8.content_excerpt: Flare is a local inference server for NVIDIA SM120/SM121 GPUs, built for long conversations, coding agents, and repeated tool use. Its goal is to make the memory, bandwidth, and compute in workstations and compact systems such as DGX Spark go further, while keeping generation responsive. This is a research prototype, and is made available via open-source to enable technical collaboration and collect early feedback. Embrace the standard PyTorch ecosystem at build time; serve from Rust. Ignition uses PyTorch, Transformers, and FlashInfer/b12x to load models, tune kernels, compile forwards, and capture CUDA graphs into a runtime package. Helios, the Rust runtime, serves that package without Python. Compilation and graph capture finish before serving. Build on the model ecosystem. Reuse canonical model implementations wherever their dataflow fits, and specialize the parts that need different layouts or execution. Model development keeps the tools and libraries that make the Python ecosystem productive. Make memory and state explicit. Plan buffers and execution capacities ahead of time. Treat conversation state—including recurrent state alongside KV caches—as a whole, so reuse, branching, and resuming preserve it correctly. Keep the runtime small and shared. Model recipes own model computation; the runtime owns scheduling, cache storage, and request handling. A focused hardware and kernel stack keeps those boundaries manageable. vLLM covers a much broader range of models, hardware

e7aea804d1201fff.content_excerpt: Every few months, someone points out that the world is drowning in idle compute. Your laptop idles at an office desk. Your phone spends most of its battery waiting in your pocket. Meanwhile, tech monopolies pour hundreds of billions of dollars into sprawling, water-guzzling data centers packed with high-end clusters to train and run modern language models. The intuitive alternative is obvious: split the model up and run it across everyone’s devices. Yet whenever people attempt decentralized AI, they run into the same brick wall. Projects like Petals and BloomBee proved you could run inference over the public internet, but they mostly approach it through pipeline parallelism—handing entire layers to individual machines. The trouble with that strategy is the entry fee. If Layer 14 requires 8 GB or 16 GB of memory, every device with only 2 GB or 4 GB of spare RAM gets locked out. The network ends up looking like a rickety chain of modest servers rather than a truly universal computing mesh. The real breakthrough isn’t distributing layer by layer. It is slicing within the sub-layers themselves. A standard Transformer block is made of two distinct computational engines: the feed-forward / MLP block and the attention mechanism. Let AI agents troubleshoot Ubuntu machines, with permissions enforced by the kernel instead of the prompt. A plan written the way a hijacked model would, as maatctl shows it to the person reviewing it: the hidden escape codes appear as text, and the invented evidence ID is flagged. The name: Ma'at was the ancient Egyptian principle of truth and balance — the standard a life was weighed against, with the result recorded by Thoth. This tool weighs every proposed change before allowing it, and keeps the record. maat is an open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and toolkit for diagnosing and repairing Ubuntu systems with AI agents: Status: developer preview. The server, CLIs, actuator, audit trail and benchmark harness are implemented in Go and tested. On an Ubuntu 24.04 VM (arm64), the strict snap's self-test passes all six checks that prove confinement: it reads the journal and lists 502 systemd units, yet creating any internet socket fails with EACCES , writing to your home directory is refused, and AppArmor itself (not polkit) refuses RestartUnit . The full human loop has also been run there: a proposal from the confined server, review in maatctl , refusal of tampered plans, a polkit prompt, apply and verify, and trail verification.
